extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for determining when courts should require clear congressional authorization before upholding an agency’s claim to broad regulatory power (the Major Questions Doctrine). Identifies triggers, contextual factors, and textual limits courts use to decide whether an agency’s asserted authority implicates a 'major question.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear congressional authorization for major questions
rubrics_metrics.description: When an agency claims power to make decisions of vast 'economic and political significance,' it must point to 'clear congressional authorization' to regulate in that manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Major Questions Doctrine functions as a clear-statement rule: vague statutory grants are insufficient; courts require an unambiguous textual authorization for highly consequential agency action. (See Utility Air, ante, at 17, 19; text: 'point to “clear congressional authorization”').

rubrics_metrics.name: Political-significance / national debate trigger
rubrics_metrics.description: The doctrine applies when the agency claims authority to resolve a matter of great 'political significance' or when the issue is the subject of an 'earnest and profound debate across the country.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts treat as 'major' those questions that are politically fraught or widely debated (examples cited: Gonzales v. Oregon; NFIB v. OSHA). Presence of robust national debate or contested social policy weighs in favor of requiring clear congressional delegation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic-significance / large economic effect trigger
rubrics_metrics.description: The doctrine applies when the agency’s action would regulate 'a significant portion of the American economy' or require 'billions of dollars in spending' by private persons or entities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look to whether the asserted power affects broad sectors or imposes enormous economic costs (examples: King v. Burwell; Utility Air; cases involving tobacco regulation, telecommunications, housing, etc.). Large-scale economic impact is a sign a clear statement is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intrusion into traditional state domains / federalism trigger
rubrics_metrics.description: The doctrine may apply where an agency seeks to 'intrud[e] into an area that is the particular domain of state law.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When federal agency action risks displacing or regulating matters traditionally left to States, courts require certainty about Congress’s intent before finding delegation of such authority. The federalism canon and major questions doctrine often operate together.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration-and-rejection by Congress
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence that Congress has 'considered and rejected' legislation authorizing something similar counsels skepticism toward an agency’s claim of authority to accomplish that same result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failed or repeatedly rejected bills addressing the same regulatory scheme (e.g., cap-and-trade proposals) are a meaningful sign that Congress did not intend to delegate that power implicitly to the agency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unprecedented or novel agency power requires explicit language
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed delegation of 'unprecedented power[s]' or powers of 'supreme delicacy and importance' will not be presumed from doubtful or uncertain statutory language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts should not infer high-stakes delegations from ambiguous text; historically recognized need for 'clear and direct' language when agencies claim such powers (citing ICC precedent and Industrial Union Dept.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency expertise mismatch as a negative indicium
rubrics_metrics.description: When an agency lacks 'comparative expertise' in the technical or policy domain implicated by the claimed authority, that supports the presumption Congress would not have delegated the matter to that agency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider agency admissions about lacking necessary technical/policy expertise (e.g., EPA acknowledging it needs expertise 'not traditionally needed in EPA regulatory development'). Such a mismatch favors requiring explicit congressional authorization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical nonuse and failed attempts to secure authority
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency’s longstanding practice of not exercising a claimed power, together with unsuccessful attempts to obtain that authority from Congress, reinforces skepticism that Congress granted the power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The absence of prior exercise of authority across decades and efforts to secure an express grant from Congress (unsuccessful) are meaningful; precedent treats nonuse as evidence against delegation (citing Bunte Brothers, Brown & Williamson).

rubrics_metrics.name: Textual vagueness is insufficient to support broad power
rubrics_metrics.description: Broad or vague statutory phrases (e.g., 'system of emission reduction') do not, without context, constitute the clear authorization the doctrine requires.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts should assess whether terms are empty vessels when shorn of context; mere definitional possibilities do not satisfy the clear-statement requirement. The presence of many possible meanings militates against inferring major delegations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish between compliance mechanisms and substantive policymaking
rubrics_metrics.description: Authorizations that permit regulated parties to use mechanisms (like emissions trading) to comply with a preset statutory limit are different from authorizing an agency to set the substantive limit itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the statute sets the limit (e.g., statutory cap or objective scientific criterion), market mechanisms to comply may be permissible. But authorizing an agency to determine the numerical limit or the overall nationwide mix of energy sources is a major question requiring clear congressional direction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of clear-statement/ambiguity-canons analogy
rubrics_metrics.description: The major questions doctrine operates like other clear-statement rules (e.g., those protecting against retroactive legislation or abrogation of sovereign immunity): it requires express words or an insurmountable implication before courts find delegation of significant constitutional consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the same skepticism and demand for clarity as with retroactivity and sovereign-immunity canons; where rights or core structural constitutional principles are implicated, courts look for express congressional language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption against delegating major social/economic policy decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Judges presume Congress would not delegate to an agency the authority to settle or amend major social and economic policy decisions absent a clear indication to the contrary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This presumption draws on separation-of-powers concerns and the idea that consequential tradeoffs belong to the people’s representatives; use predecessors (e.g., MCI, Brown & Williamson) as touchstones.
